blocks.text: GTM Engineer Jobs: What Postings Actually Ask For (and What They Pay)

GTM engineer job postings grew 205% year over year. Here is what 1,000 real listings actually require, what they pay across three independent sources, and when to hire full-time versus bring in outside help.

GTM engineer job postings grew 205% year over year from 2024 to 2025, according to Bloomberry's analysis of 1,000 GTM engineering job listings, with roughly 100 new postings appearing every month by early 2026. ZoomInfo's pipeline research cites the same Bloomberry figure and adds an important detail: this is bottom-up demand, driven by practitioners who already need the role, not a top-down executive mandate to create one.

If you are trying to hire for this role, or trying to land one, the postings themselves are the best signal of what companies actually want, more reliable than any title debate. This guide covers what real job descriptions ask for, what they pay, where they show up, and how to tell a good posting from a lazy copy-paste of a RevOps template.
If you have not read what the role actually is first, our GTM engineer resource covers what a GTM engineer does, how it differs from RevOps, the skills path, and salary data in more depth.
What GTM engineer job postings actually require

Bloomberry's analysis of 1,000 postings breaks down the tools and skills that show up most often. The pattern: heavy tool literacy, moderate code requirement, and a track record of owning outbound or pipeline infrastructure.

The average posting asks for 4.11 years of experience, per the same analysis. That number is lower than it looks: because the title itself is new, most candidates are counting adjacent experience (RevOps, sales engineering, marketing ops, or backend development) rather than years spent literally holding this job title, since the title has not existed long enough to produce many candidates with 4+ years in the role itself.

What good and bad postings actually look like

A posting copy-pasted from a RevOps template usually asks for CRM administration experience and says nothing about scripting, APIs, or Clay. That is a mismatch waiting to happen: you will get RevOps candidates who cannot build the pipeline you actually need, or GTM engineers who apply and then get bored administering Salesforce all day.
A posting that reflects what this role actually needs usually includes:

A named system, not a vague mandate. "Own our outbound enrichment pipeline in Clay" reads very differently than "help scale our go-to-market motion." The first tells a real candidate exactly what they would be doing Monday morning.
A stated tool stack. Naming Clay, HubSpot or Salesforce, and whichever automation layer you use (Zapier, n8n, or custom scripts) filters out candidates who only know point-and-click tools.

An honest coding bar. If the role genuinely needs someone who can write a Python script or a SQL query unsupervised, say so. If it does not, do not scare off good no-code-first candidates by overstating the requirement, since roughly six in ten postings in Bloomberry's dataset lean on spreadsheet and no-code fluency rather than a hard coding requirement.
A reporting line. State whether this reports into RevOps, marketing, or sales, since that answers the "will I be doing real building or mostly admin work" question candidates are actually asking.

AI agent ownership, if it applies. If part of the job is building or maintaining an agent that drafts outbound or qualifies replies, list it explicitly. It is increasingly part of the role, and candidates who want to build agents will self-select toward postings that say so directly.

What GTM engineer jobs pay

Salary data for this exact title is still thin because the role is new, so treat every figure below as a directional range rather than a fixed number, and read the ranges from more than one source before anchoring an offer or an ask.

The Bloomberry median and the Levels.fyi median land within about $5,000 of each other despite being pulled from completely different data sets (job postings versus self-reported compensation), which is a reasonable sign the true median sits somewhere in the $125,000 to $135,000 range for the title broadly, with senior and equity-heavy roles at well-funded startups pulling the average well above that.
Where these postings actually show up

Company career pages and LinkedIn carry the largest share of listings, since most hiring for this title still happens at venture-backed startups that post directly rather than routing through a traditional job board. Our roundup of the best AI engineer job boards covers the adjacent boards worth checking too, several of which now carry GTM engineer and GTM-adjacent listings alongside pure AI-engineering roles, since the two hiring pools increasingly overlap.

If postings under the exact title "GTM engineer" are scarce in your market or your company is too early-stage to justify the title, search adjacent titles instead: RevOps engineer, growth engineer, and sales automation engineer all describe overlapping work, and reading the responsibilities section rather than the title is the more reliable filter either way.
Should you post a GTM engineer role, or bring in outside help first

ZoomInfo's research frames this well: demand for the role is bottom-up, meaning a practitioner already hit a wall that only custom infrastructure can solve, not a top-down decision to add headcount for its own sake. Their read is that a dedicated, full-time hire tends to make the most sense once a company reaches Series B or beyond with a GTM team of 50 or more people generating enough recurring pipeline work to justify a full-time salary.

Below that size, most teams are better served by bringing in an agency to build and hand off the GTM engineering system rather than posting a full-time role you are not yet ready to keep busy, or by a fractional engagement that builds the initial pipeline and stays on to maintain it part-time. A full-time hire sitting mostly idle between build cycles is a worse outcome than a focused engagement that ships the same pipeline in weeks instead of a multi-month hiring process.

What this means for you

Read the tool list before the title. A posting that names Clay, HubSpot, and a real automation layer is describing this role accurately; one that only mentions CRM administration is really a RevOps posting with a trendier title.
4.11 years is a soft bar, not a hard one. Most strong candidates are transferring in from RevOps, sales engineering, or backend development, not applying with 4+ years under the exact title.

Anchor salary to a range, not a single number. $127,500 to $132,000 is the reasonable median across two independent data sources; senior and equity-heavy roles at well-funded startups run well above that.

Company stage should drive the hire-versus-agency decision. Series B and beyond with a large GTM team usually justifies a full-time hire; earlier-stage teams are usually better served bringing in outside help to build the system first rather than carrying a full-time salary before the pipeline exists.
List AI agent ownership explicitly if it is part of the job. It is increasingly core to the role, and burying it in vague language filters out exactly the candidates who want to do that work.
FAQ

How many GTM engineer jobs are open right now? Bloomberry's analysis of the space found postings grew 205% year over year from 2024 to 2025, with roughly 100 new listings appearing monthly by early 2026. The exact live count shifts constantly since most postings run on individual company career pages rather than a single centralized board.

What skills do most GTM engineer job postings require? SQL and Python each appear in 38% of postings, per Bloomberry's dataset, alongside heavier tool requirements: HubSpot (52%), Outreach (49%), Salesforce (45%), and Zapier (39%), with Clay as the single most-cited tool overall.

Do I need to know how to code to get hired for this role? Not always. Roughly six in ten postings in the Bloomberry dataset lean on spreadsheet and no-code fluency (Clay, Zapier) rather than a hard coding requirement, though SQL and Python each still appear in about a third of listings, so knowing at least basic SQL meaningfully widens which postings you qualify for.

What does a GTM engineer job actually pay? Bloomberry's posting analysis found a $127,500 median, and Levels.fyi independently reports a $132,000 median total comp, a close enough match across two different data sources to treat that range as a reasonable center. Senior roles at well-funded startups run considerably higher: a real, now-closed Vercel posting listed $180,000 to $310,000/yr OTE plus equity.

Where should I actually look for GTM engineer job postings? Company career pages and LinkedIn carry the largest share, since most hiring happens at venture-backed startups posting directly. If listings under the exact title are scarce, search RevOps engineer, growth engineer, and sales automation engineer instead, and judge postings by their responsibilities section rather than the title.

Should a small company hire a full-time GTM engineer or bring in outside help? ZoomInfo's research suggests a dedicated full-time hire tends to make sense around Series B and beyond, once a GTM team reaches roughly 50 or more people generating enough ongoing pipeline work to justify the salary. Earlier-stage teams are usually better served bringing in a GTM engineering agency or fractional engineer to build the initial system, since a full-time hire with gaps between build cycles is a worse outcome than a focused build-and-handoff engagement.

How is a GTM engineer job different from a RevOps job posting? A GTM engineer posting should name a specific system to own (an enrichment pipeline, an integration, an agent) and a real tool stack (Clay, HubSpot or Salesforce, an automation layer), while a RevOps posting centers on CRM administration, process design, and forecasting. If a posting only describes admin work but uses the GTM engineer title, read it as a RevOps role that has not updated its job description.

Sources: Bloomberry, "I analyzed 1000 GTM Engineering jobs, here is what I learned", ZoomInfo Pipeline, "GTM Engineer: Role, Skills, Salary, and Career Path in 2026", SyncGTM, "GTM Engineer Jobs in 2026: What Hiring Teams Want"
